blocks.text: Lucy Letby - Examination-in-chief day 1: Background and general topics
CONTENTS
MS LUCY LETBY (sworn)
Examination-in-chief by MR MYERS
Tuesday, 2 May 2023
(In the absence of the jury)
Just by way of information, the reasons for my ruling on Friday will be made available to you later today.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, thank you, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: (In the presence of the jury)
MS LUCY LETBY (sworn)
Examination-in-chief by MR MYERS
Ms Letby, would you give the court your full name, please?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. Lucy Letby.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And what's your date of birth, Ms Letby?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: 4 January 1990.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: So you're now 33 years old?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: In the period that we're looking at in the most detail in this case, between June 2015 through to June 2016, you were 25/26 years old?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's right, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Which part of the country were you born in, Ms Letby?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Herefordshire.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: I want you to tell us a little bit about that and becoming a nurse first. That's the first thing I'm going to ask you about.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Are your family from Herefordshire?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, they are, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Whereabouts in Herefordshire did you grow up, not the precise address but the area?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Within Hereford city centre itself.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And who did you grow up with in your house?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's just myself and my mum and dad.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And did you go to school locally?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Where did you go to college?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I went to the local sixth form college.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: When was it that you first knew you wanted to be a nurse?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I've always wanted to work with children but it was towards the end of secondary school that I thought I wanted to do nursing and then picked A level subjects that would best support that career.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: All right. Did you have to go to university to study nursing?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Is that something new for someone in your family?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I was the first person in the family to go to university, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: You're doing well with your voice. It's important to keep it up. You've heard other witnesses being asked to do that so make sure you speak across to the jury and keep your voice as loud as you can.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Where did you do your nursing degree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: At the University of Chester.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And can you help us, how long is the course that you take to become a nurse?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's a three-year degree programme.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And do you spend all of it in the university or are bits of it spent out in hospitals?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's 50/50. Part of it is theory-based at the university and then you have numerous placements throughout that time in different clinical areas to give you experience of different areas of nursing.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Did you ever get any familiarity with the Countess of Chester before you went to work there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, the majority of my placements, clinical placements, were at the Countess of Chester.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And any particular unit on the Countess of Chester?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, either the children's ward or the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: When did you qualify as a band 5 nurse, Ms Letby?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: September 2011.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And is that -- does that coincide with the end of your degree or was there some further training you had to do to become band 5?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, that was the end of my degree training.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Over the period of 2015 to 2016 -- we you know we're looking at a number of babies in this indictment and you understand that, don't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: There's 17 of them.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: But could you put a figure on the number of babies you cared for over that 12-month period?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Probably hundreds.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Hundreds?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And did you care for them?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Did you ever do anything that was meant to hurt any of them?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I only ever did my best to care for them.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Did you ever want to hurt any baby you looked after?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, that's completely against everything that being a nurse is: I'm there to help and to care, not to harm.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: All right. I want to ask you next about the period in fact after you were removed from clinical duties. So we're looking at the period in July 2016 when you were moved away from clinical duties.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Why did you think you were being put in a non-clinical role that July?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That there'd been an increased mortality rate on the unit and as a result numerous members of staff were having to go through a competency check and redo their competencies and that would be starting with myself.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And how did you come to believe that is what was happening?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's what I was told.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And who were you told that by?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: By management within the hospital and the executive team.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: That you were going to be undergoing training or testing in your competencies?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Is it something you had volunteered to do?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Is it something you were keen to do?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: How did you feel when you were removed from clinical duties and were told that your competencies were going to be checked like this?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I was devastated.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Why were you devastated?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Because I've always prided myself on being very competent and the fact that potentially I hadn't been competent in something really, really affected me, and to be taken away from the job that I loved, it was very difficult.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: When you say it really affected you -- could you convey to the ladies and gentlemen of the jury the extent of that when you say it really affected you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It was just -- it was life-changing in that moment.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: I was taken away from the support system that I had on the unit, I was then put into a non-clinical role that I didn't enjoy. I had to pretend to a lot of people that that was a voluntary process, which it wasn't, and from a self-confidence point of view it completely -- well, it made me question everything about myself.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Right. When was it, so far as you can recall, you first discovered that you were being held responsible for harm to babies on the unit or their deaths?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not until the September of 2016.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: What event was it in September 2016 that led to you discovering that you were being held responsible for deaths of babies?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I received a letter from the Royal College of Nursing in which they had been informed that actually the true reason for my redeployment was because I was being held responsible.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: We're thinking about -- do you remember roughly what date that would have been that you received that letter?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not the precise day but maybe which month.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It was September.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: September 2016?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And what was going on that meant you received that letter at about that time? What was taking place or about to start?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So I was looking at putting in a grievance procedure.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: About what?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: About how I'd been redeployed from the unit and the information that I'd been given in relation to that.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Did you have any idea how many babies you were being held responsible for harming or for their deaths?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: How did it make you feel when you received the news that you were being held responsible?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, it was sickening, it was -- I knowledge couldn't believe it.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: I want you to describe how best you can -- it may not be easy, but describe as bet you can what it felt like to have that being said about you, Ms Letby, if you can.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I mean, it was devastating. I don't think there's -- I don't think you can be accused of anything worse than that. And... Yeah, I was just devastated.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Well, you tell us how it affected you, that might be another way of looking at this. What was the effect of this on you, what happened?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I just changed as a person: my mental health deteriorated and I felt very isolated from my friends and family on the unit and...
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Just pausing there, when you say isolated, of course you'd been removed from the neonatal unit. Had you had friends on the neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, a lot of friends. We were a very supportive unit as well. Regardless of whether we were personal friends, we were a very supportive nursing team (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: When you moved on to -- sorry, I interrupted you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's okay.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: When you moved to a non-clinical role and you were being told that you'd undergo the competency testing, were you able to explain that to other people on the unit?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No. So at that time, the hospital advised me not to communicate with anybody on the unit and to sort of go with the
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: pretence that it was a voluntary secondment and it was identified at that time that there were two or three friends that I would be able to speak to but otherwise I was not to have contact with anyone on the unit.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: You say it was identified there were two or three friends you could speak to, who were they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It was [Nurse E], [Dr A] and Minna Lappalainen.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: [Nurse E]?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: [Dr A]?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And Minna Lappalainen?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: You'd said that you had felt isolated, you had been describing how it felt when you learned you were being blamed for a death or deaths. You made a reference to your mental health. Did you have to go and seek any assistance with how it affected you, mentally speaking?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I did, yes, I went to my GP. I wasn't sleeping, I wasn't eating. I just had a complete change in my whole life and I was starting on some anti-depressants at that point, which I remain on now.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: So did the GP put you on antidepressants?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: If it doesn't seem too obvious a question, what's that for? What were you given them for? What state were you in?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: They diagnosed me with depression and anxiety at that time.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And you say you've remained on that medication?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And are you receiving that now?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Do you take any other medication at the moment?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I also take medication to help with sleep -- yes, I am unable to sleep without medication.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: How bad did the negative feelings get so far as you're concerned about yourself, how bad?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There were times when I didn't want to live.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And what did you want to do? What did you think of doing?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: To myself?
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I thought of killing myself.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Had you done anything wrong?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Why did you think of killing yourself, somebody might ask?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Because of what was being inferred.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: How hard had you worked to become a nurse?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Very hard.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: How much did it matter to you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: My job was my life. It was... It was everything.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: How did it feel to have that taken away and be held responsible for the deaths of babies you'd cared for?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I can't put that into words. It's just... My whole world just stopped.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Have you ever been able to recover your kind of mental ease after all of this started?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I think it's just progressively got worse.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: How hard is it to cope with what you're being accused of?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's very difficult.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: If you think back to the young woman you were when you were 25 or 26, before you were taken off the unit, before you were being blamed for what happened, are you the same person in yourself now as you were then?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I think it's completely changed everything, a lot about me and about my life, about the hopes that I had for the future, everything has just gone.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Where have you been living since November 2020? What type of place?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So I've been remanded in prison since that time.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: That's since your third arrest in November 2020?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I've been in four different prisons since then.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: I'm not going to ask you the locations of any prison, Ms Letby, I don't invite you to do that. But before that first arrest in July 2018, had you ever been in trouble with the police before for anything?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you a little bit about the experience of arrest and prison. When I do that, I make it absolutely clear that we are grateful to the officers at court and those who bring you to and from court and the cell staff for the care you have received. That's the same for you isn't it, Ms Letby?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It is, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: So we are just looking at the effect of events on you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There is nothing at all critical about the people caring for you --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: -- and we are grateful for that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You were arrested for the first time on 3 July 2018?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Had you ever experienced anything like that before?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Are you able to just describe in simple terms the impact of arrest and that process on you? Let me start with this: how did you know the police were coming that day?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: What's the first you knew?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: When there was a loud knocking at the door at 6 o'clock in the morning by the police.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: You were at home in 41 Westbourne road Chester; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I was, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Were you on your own there, as it happens?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, my father was staying with me at that point, so he was there as well.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Had you any idea the police were coming that day?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, none at all.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: So when they came, what happened with you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: They told me that I was being arrested for multiple counts of murder and attempted murder and then they quickly handcuffed me and took me away.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: All right. And you were taken to a police station; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In my pyjamas, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And over the next 3 days you were interviewed at various times?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And we've asked DS Stonier about that. Again, the way that was done is just the way the police deal with it and that's not critical of them for the process they followed.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: When that process had ended after the 3 days of interviews, were you released from police custody?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I was, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: On bail?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And did you have to live anywhere in particular after that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, as a part of my bail conditions, I wasn't allowed to return to my house in Chester, so from that point on I then lived with my parents back in Hereford.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Is that where you were living when we come to the time of your second arrest on 10 June 2019?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It is, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And on that occasion did you know the police were coming that day?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, it was a mirror image of the time before. It was just loud banging and knocking at the door and we opened it to find police there.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: It may be difficult taking your mind back to these things, Ms Letby, but so that the jury understand, what was the impact on you, the banging and the being arrested again, if you're able to say?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It was just the most -- the scariest thing I've ever been there. It not only happened once, it happened twice and then a third time, and it's just... It's just traumatised me, I just...
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: The third time was on 10 November 2020?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And that's the time after which you weren't actually released, you were kept in prison?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And you've been in prison since then?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I have, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: When you say it traumatised you, we've heard that you're on medication. So we can understand, has it left you sensitive to particular things, so the jury understand, certain things that affect you in certain ways?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. The biggest way it's affected me is I just -- I'm very sensitive to any noise, any unexpected change or new people. I'm easily startled, easily frightened of things.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Were you like that before the arrests began?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, not at all.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And have you received psychological support in prison and at court, as we've been going forwards?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I have, yes. I've been diagnosed with PTSD in direct relation to the arrests, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Right. And so far as being at court is concerned, again, we're grateful to all those who care for you and bring you to and from court, but without going into the businesses of locations, how long is the trip to court each morning for you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's usually around an hour and a half each way.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And the same in the evening?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It is yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: What time do you normally get up before you come to court?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: About half past 5.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Where do you have your breakfast?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I have my breakfast when I arrive here at court, we leave about 6.30 in the morning and I eat when I arrive here. I also get quite bad travel sickness so I wait and eat my breakfast when I've arrived here.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: What time do you get back to the prison in the evenings as a general rule?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Usually around 7 pm.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: We have all seen various notes that were taken by the police that you had written. You know the notes I'm referring to, don't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: We're going to look at a number of them as we're going through your evidence, Ms Letby. Not all in one go but at various points. But just to help the jury with this, in general, are you the sort of person who writes things down in notes, on notes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it's something I've done my whole life. That is my way of dealing with things, just day to day. That is what I've always done, I've always written things down.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And do you throw them away always when you've written things down?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I never throw anything away. I have difficulties throwing things away, everything is just kept.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Right. Let's look at the note which we've got in the images the prosecution gave us. It's the prosecution images, page 18. We'll see if Mr Murphy can help us with that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We'll look at a close-up in a moment, but I'm going to ask you some questions about the note that's on the right-hand side of this page, Ms Letby. Were the notes like this in your house or is just how they have been arranged for the purposes of photographing it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, that's how it's been arranged.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: So the police have set it out so we can see it for the photograph?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Do you know hen it was -- can we go to page 19, in fact, Mr Murphy, so we can see the note more clearly? Thank you. We'll have a look at this in a moment, Ms Letby.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But do you recall when it was that you would have written this, what period of time?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: After my removal from the unit in 2016 and prior to my arrest, this time.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Do you know any precise date when you wrote it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: We're going to have a look at what's written here. Look at the top if you would. It says, "Not good enough"; yes? Why have you written "not good enough" and underlined it, if you can tell us, just doing the best you can, all right? Why have you written "not good enough" and underlined it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think that's the overwhelming thought and feeling that I had about myself at that point, that I wasn't good enough.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And why did you think you weren't good enough?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Because of the way people had made me feel.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Had you actually done anything wrong to hurt any babies?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: How were you feeling because of the things that people were saying about you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I felt an immense responsibility. I thought that I had been incompetent or done something wrong that had harmed children.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: When we're looking at the notes, do you -- is it the case you've always written everything we see on them on one occasion or are they sometimes written at different times, bits of the notes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It can be both.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Right. We're going to track across this. It says on the left:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "There are no words."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That seems to carry on on the left-hand side:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "I can't breathe, I can't focus."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Perhaps you could read it, Ms Letby.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The objection isn't to my learned friend reading the words, it's to him interpreting that one bit follows another. I'd rather the witness said which bit was written by --
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's fine.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: "There are no words." What would come after "there are no words" when you look at that?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: The text to the left-hand side, "I can't breathe, I can't focus".
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Overwhelming fear and panic."
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And what's that describing when it says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "There are no words. I can't breathe, I can't focus. Overwhelming fear and panic"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's how I felt about my life at that moment in time.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Under that it says, "I haven't done anything wrong".
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Why does it say, "I haven't done anything wrong"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Because I haven't done anything wrong.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Who are you writing this note for or to?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It wasn't to anyone, it was just me processing my thoughts. It was never meant to be read by anyone.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Can you help us with why it says "police investigation"
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: on the left-hand side under that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Because I knew that, ultimately, the worst-case scenario would be that the police would be involved, and that was something that had been threatened by the hospital.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Why under that does it say, if you can help us, "Slander, discrimination"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's how I felt that the trust and hospital -- that's how I felt they were towards me, that it was slander and discrimination.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And what was slander and discrimination?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The allegations.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Under that, it says, "All getting too much". What follows on from "all getting too much" when we look at the note, if anything follows on?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Um... "Everything's taken over my life".
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Um... I think it's:
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: "... everyone and I feel very alone and scared."
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: All right. Is that how you were feeling?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: I want to look across to the right-hand side, if we could, for the time being. Reading down the right:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "I'm an awful person. I pay every day for that right now."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You tell me if I read anything incorrectly by the way.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Why are you saying:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "I'm an awful person. I pay every day for that right now"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Because at that time I did feel that I must be an awful person to have made any mistakes that had harmed anyone and that I was paying the price for that by what had happened to me.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And what had happened to you at this point, as best as you can remember?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That I'd been taken away from the job that I loved and accused of things that I just hadn't done.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Underneath it says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "I'll never have children or marry."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can you read the next bit, "I'll never..."?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "... never know what it's like to have a family."
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Right. Why were you saying that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Because at that time I couldn't see any future for myself. I couldn't imagine what my life was going to be or that I'd ever have a future.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: This is all your handwriting; do you agree?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It is, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Why have you written "no hope" at an angle towards the side of the note on the right-hand side?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Because there were times when I didn't have any hope.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: My whole situation felt hopeless at times.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And at the same kind of angle a bit below that it says "despair"; can you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: What is that describing?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Again, one of the emotions that I was feeling at that time.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Just to the left of "despair" it says -- does it say:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Hate myself so much for what this has..."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And then it's hard to read, we can perhaps scroll down a bit. Let's see if that follows through with anything. Thank you, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Does it follow with anything or does it just run out at "what this has"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I believe it just runs out there, I think.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: It says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Hate myself so much for what this has..."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And then we can see a circle heavily in ink and the word "hate" in it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Why did you say:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Hate myself so much for what this has..."?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Why did you say that in the note?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Because at that time I did hate myself.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: You've said in the note:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "I haven't done anything wrong."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So people might think, well, how do you hate yourself if you haven't done anything wrong?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Because I was made to feel that I had done something wrong, so potentially -- I though I had been incompetent in some way.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: What kind of mental state were you in at the time you were writing this note?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not good at all.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Had you been to see the doctor by this time or not or do you not know?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I couldn't say, but throughout that period my mental health was poor.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: How well were you coping with the situation you were in?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I did my best, but it was difficult in the circumstances with the isolation that I felt and -- yeah, it was difficult.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: We know you were first arrested in July 2018. How long a period was this kind of thing going on for and these sort of thoughts going on for?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Two years.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Carry on looking across to the left-hand side again now.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Following from where it says -- can you see:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "How can I get through it?"
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Do you see that, Ms Letby?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: "How can I get through it?"
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: What's directly under that, please? Could you read the next --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "How will things ever be like they were?"
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And then if we carry on on the left-hand side and it says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "I don't deserve to live."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Is that what it says?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Then does it say:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "I killed them on purpose because I'm not good enough"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Was there anything that follows on from that? "Because I'm not good enough", does it stop or does it carry on?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "I'm not good enough to care for them and I'm a horrible, evil person."
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Right. When you say "kill them on purpose", does that mean you've gone and done something intentionally to harm them and kill them?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: What are you meaning when you say:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "I killed them on purpose because I'm not good enough to care for them"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That I hadn't been good enough and I'd in some way failed in my duties and my competencies.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Why did you think you hadn't or you might not have been good enough?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Because that was the suggestion throughout, that I had to redo competencies, that I'd been removed from the unit. I felt that I'd done something wrong. That's what was insinuated to me, that my competencies had to be rechecked.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: It says, "I don't deserve mum and dad".
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And then:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "World is better off [is that] without me"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: What's the bit that follows that "without me"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That says Tom and Matt, who are my cousins.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Is that one sentence or is that different things?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I've written there:
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: "I don't deserve mum and dad, Tom and Matt."
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And I think, "World is better off without me", is separator to that.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: So you say you don't deserve your mum or your dad or your cousins and you have also said the world is better off without you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And it says at the bottom, "I am evil, I did this". Why did you say that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Because I felt at that time if I'd done something wrong and I didn't know I had done that, I must be such an awful, evil person if I'd made mistakes and not known.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: But we've seen at the top of the note, the actual heading of it underlined is "Not good enough". So what did you believe had happened or you'd done or might have done?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That somehow I'd been incompetent and that I'd done something wrong which had led to -- affecting those babies.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Just looking on the right-hand side at an angle, it says, "Panic, fear, lost"; do you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: What's that describing?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That was how I was feeling.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Under "hate" it says, "I did this". Can you see, "I did this"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: What do you mean when the note says, "I did this"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That I felt I must be responsible in some way.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: You've also written, "Why me?" If you're able to, can you help us with why it says, "Why me"? If you can.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Because I didn't understand why it was happening to me.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: I thought I'd always been competent, I'd always done my best. I couldn't understand why it was happening to me.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Looking back on this now, as much as you can, how were you coping with the situation you were in at the time you wrote this note?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think, looking back on it now, I was really struggling. This is a way of me expressing everything that I felt at that time that I wasn't able to say to anyone else.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: You told us earlier that writing things down is a way that you deal with them; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Writing them down in words on bits of paper like this, is that something you've done in the past?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it's what I do regularly. It just can be on any piece of paper, just randomly, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Well, as I've said, there's other notes and papers and we will return to them as we go along so we can have a look at what you have said and you help us with bits of them as best as you can. Just to assist you, and also to assist the court and the ladies and gentlemen of the jury, just so we know how we're going to deal with your evidence, if we can, with your assistance we're going to go through all the kind of general background and pieces of evidence to do with things the police found or how the unit worked, general type of material. That might take a little while. Then when we've done that, we'll turn to looking at the babies on the indictment to which the allegations relate. All right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: That's just so we can all keep track of where we're going and how we'll deal with that. We can take the note down, please.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: How does it feel inside yourself when, for instance, I ask you questions about the arrest process and you're talking about banging on the door and things?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's uncomfortable for me.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Looking at the notes and things, how does that feel?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The same. I'm a very private person and those weren't meant to ever be read.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: If you don't mind me saying, however private you are, Ms Letby, can you keep your voice up so we can all hear what you're saying now? Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you next a little bit more about the Countess of Chester neonatal unit and some aspects of the work that goes on there. All right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Can you remember when it was that you first experienced working at the Countess of Chester neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. I had a placement there during my nurse training.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: I think it was in 2010. That was the first time I'd ever been on a neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Do you remember when it was that you started there fulltime as a qualified nurse?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, January 2012.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And you'd have been a band 5 nurse at that point?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's right, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And when you started in January 2012, what levels of babies would you be qualified to care for?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So at that time, when you first qualify, you're only able to look after special care and high-dependency babies.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: We're familiar with the unit and the nurseries. Which are nurseries the special care and the high-dependency babies would be in?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Predominantly nurseries 3 and 4.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Right. During the time that you worked on the neonatal unit, was there a system where you continued training and attended courses?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, you continue training throughout your career, really.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: How much did you value being a nurse?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Oh, massively, it was everything.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And caring for babies?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. And I always strived to go on every course possible, to try and be the best that I could.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Did you ever play a part in training or helping to guide other people who wanted to be nurses?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I did, yes. Part of my role would be to support further junior band 5s coming into the unit and I was also a mentor for student nurses at the university as well.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Just so we understand a little bit more, what does being a mentor for student nurses involve?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You undergo a mentorship qualification. So I went to the university and completed a mentorship module, which means then when student nurses come to the unit you are then their sole mentor, they work with you, you're responsible for their paperwork and their competency assessments.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Did you become a mentor?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I did, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: When did you qualify as a mentor?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Um... I think it was fairly early on in my career.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Perhaps 2012 it would have been.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Just remember dates as best as you can. No one is expecting every detail to come to mind. Fairly early on is when you recall.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: How did you feel about working with students when they came on?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I really enjoyed that aspect.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Do you know how many you acted as a mentor for?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Across the whole time frame?
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Yes, over the years you worked there.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Probably five or six.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: We saw when we were dealing with the case of [Baby O] and [Baby P], there was a student nurse called Rebecca Morgan who was with you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Was that part of the mentorship scheme?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: What sort of things would she be doing whilst she's with you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So she would be undergoing a lot of the care for the baby under my supervision and with my guidance.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And where is she when she's doing that in relation to you, Ms Letby? Where would she be?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It would depend on the sort of stage of their training that that student was at. But usually they're directly with me, they would be under direct supervision.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: That's training of other people and being a mentor with them. I asked you about training that you could undertake. I'm going to ask you about something we've heard of now and we're familiar with and that's QIS, qualification specialty.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: What does that mean once you get your QIS?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That means then that you are qualified to look after intensive care babies.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Right. Does that mean it covers all levels of care for babies?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: At that point you can then care for any level of care that's needed, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And you got your QIS did you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Which meant that you could look after intensive care babies?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: What did you have to do to become QIS authorised or qualified, whatever the terminology is?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's a university module that involves lectures, various assessments, both written assignments and practical assessments, and then I did a placement at Liverpool Women's Hospital, which is the level 3 unit, and that's where you get the hands-on clinical experience in intensive care.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: When did you start the training for this QIS?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think it was towards the end of 2014.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Right. How much time does it take to do the training and then be qualified in specialty?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Around, I think it's around 6 months.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Do you recall when it was that you would have been qualified to then start looking after intensive care babies?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think it was around the March/April time of 2015.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And the period we're looking at in this case is from June 2015 approximately, around that period?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: So you were QIS by March/April 2015?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And that meant you could then care for the sickest babies on the unit, is that correct --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: -- or those requiring the most intensive care?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Had all the nurses on the neonatal unit got their QIS?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Do you recall who did have it at your level in terms of band 5s?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: At that time there was myself and one other band 5 nurse that had the QIS training.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Who was that one other band 5 nurse?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Bernie Butterworth.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Whilst we go forwards in the period we're looking at, did any other band 5 nurse get QIS whilst you were still on the unit?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Shelley Tomlins.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And the band 6 nurses, they will be QIS?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: They are, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: So at the time we're looking at we've got the band 6s who are QIS. Who are the shift leaders, what band of nurse?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's always a band 6.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Of the band 5s, you and Bernadette Butterworth were QIS?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And Shelley Tomlins became QIS?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: QIS. If you are QIS, what does that mean about the type of work you're given on the unit?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Predominantly you're allocated to the high-dependency or intensive care babies. Because of the skill mix on the unit it tends to be that you have two bands 6s, a high grade band 5, and a lower band 5 who doesn't have the intensive care course.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: If we pause there a moment. You said "because of the skill mix"; what are you talking about, the skill mix -- you say you have two band 6 --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Usually generally on a shift you would have two band 6s, one of which would be supernumerary and in charge, then you'd usually have a QIS band 5, like myself, and then a non-QIS trained band 5 member of staff with nursery nurses.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Over this period, June 2015 to June 2016, how much of your work, if you can just describe this, would have been the intensive care work, intensive care babies or maybe --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's predominantly what I did for that period of time.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: And why would you predominantly or your time predominantly be allocated to that? Why would you be selected for that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So partly it would be that that's how the skill mix on the unit would work, so we did have a lot of intensive care babies at that time --
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Right. Let' just go though this: a lot of intensive care babies?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: So there's a need for intensive care trained nurses?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Right. What about the fact that you'd just qualified in specialty, what did that mean about you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So when you complete training, the unit is quite proactive in putting that training to use. You are the most upto-date member of staff at that point, obviously you've brought clinical skills back from a tertiary centre, so predominantly you do tend to look after those babies to develop your skills and to bring those skills to the unit as well for other people to learn from.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: When you talk about the skill mix and who's doing what, did you always have enough QIS band 5s to cover everything that needed to be covered in terms of the babies?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, not to meet the correct guidelines, no.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Which guidelines are those?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The BAPM guidelines.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: How flexible were you able to be with requests to work when called upon?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I was very flexible. At that time I was living in hospital accommodation on the site. I didn't have a family or any commitments myself, so I was very amenable and flexible to changing shifts last minute or doing overtime and extras as needed.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: We'll have a look at where you were living in due course, but even when you had a house of your own did you cease being as flexible as that or did you remain flexible?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, it was the same.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: How much did you enjoy the intensive care work?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I did enjoy it. That was my... That was kind of my passion for that area. I enjoyed all aspects but I did enjoy the intensive care side.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Did you make it clear to the nurses who were allocating nurses to babies that that was where your interest or enjoyment lay?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, and I think all nurses on the unit have an area in some way that they prefer or excel at than other areas.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: So yeah, the staff knew that I enjoyed that area and that was where I was most happy.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Did you ever say that other areas of work were boring?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, because no aspect of my work was ever boring.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: We heard evidence from a nurse called Kathryn Percival- Calderbank who said on one occasion at least that there'd been a debate with you or an argument as to where you should be working and you made it plain you wanted to work in intensive care, although you did go where she asked you to go as it happens. Did you get involved in an argument with Kathryn Percival- Calderbank, as far as you can remember, about that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I have no recollection of that, no.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Do you recall getting in arguments with anyone about where it was you should be working?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: Did you make your feelings clear about where you preferred to work?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. As I say, I think everybody on the unit would know who preferred working in different areas. So yeah, staff knew that I'd recently done my QIS training and therefore enjoyed being in nursery 1 to develop those skills, yes.
blocks.speaker: LETBY

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you next a little bit about the paperwork and some of the tasks you deal with on the unit. My Lord, I will do that over the next 10 minutes or thereabouts, if I may, if that's suitable to the court, and then find a place to stop?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'll leave it entirely up to you, Mr Myers --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: -- and then I'll say something to the jury then about how we're going to follow the procedure thereafter.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, never.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.

blocks.text: Or hurting him or her?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, never.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MR MYERS
